STYLE: FLAT 2D VECTOR, EDITORIAL (for corporate explainers, policy, process and product lessons; calm, adult, considered)
- Real perspective, simplified: one- or two-point, every receding edge goes to its vanishing point; furniture keeps true proportions (no bloated, rounded 'app illustration' furniture, no corporate-Memphis distortion).
- Volumes are built from 3 to 4 flat, OPAQUE tone planes (base, shade, highlight, and the deep shade in contact corners). No outlines, no transparency or multiply effects for form (glass is the exception: it may show what is behind it through fill-opacity); where two planes of the same material meet, separate them by a change of tone, not a line. No shape and no gap between shapes smaller than 8 px at 1080p, so nothing thin reads as a stray line.
- Graphic economy with intent: a window is a frame, panes and the light it throws; a chair is seat, back, base and the shadow it casts. Every object keeps its one or two most telling details (the brass foot of a lamp, the seam on a cushion, the cable from a laptop).
- Strong negative space by design: large calm planes (walls, floor) against clusters of detail; the composition reads as a magazine spread, not a catalogue.
- Small real detail follows the 8 px rule: brick courses as shade-tone bands at least 8 px tall (one band per course where a course is 8 px or more, otherwise one band per two to four courses, mortar left out); glazing bars at least 8 px; anything that would be thinner (a pen, stitching, a distant cable) is left out rather than drawn thin.
- Light: One key light (the window, on the side named in the scene). Light that falls on a surface is drawn as an opaque shape in that surface's hi tone with crisp edges (window-pane patterns on the floor and table); cast shadows as opaque shapes in that surface's shade tone, all falling the same way; contact shadows in the deep tone. No gradients, no transparency.
- Texture: None. The style lives on flat, clean planes.
- Depth: Far layer: two tones per object (base and shade), lower contrast; one haze rectangle in lm-atmos over the far layer at 0.25 opacity (with glass, the only transparency this style uses). Mid: full tones. Near: full tones and the clearest edges.

ORDER
1. Work ONE set at a time. For each: write its short plan (horizon y, vanishing points, focal point, light direction and
   shadow direction, free zones for characters with their anchors, what goes in far, mid and near), draw it, run the
   quality check, fix, save its file. Only then start the next set.
2. Never reuse one set's geometry, camera or furniture layout for another: each follows its own brief.
3. Do not draw any variants until I approve the main sets.

QUALITY CHECK (run it before you reply; redraw what fails and say what you changed)
Layout:
- Layout is cinematography: the camera height, angle and staging are decided before any rendering. Plan every set as far, mid and near ground, and leave clear space for the characters on the floor and around their heads, with breathing room on the side they will face.
- Prefer a low horizon (seated or standing eye height, never a high bird's-eye) so the room is not mostly empty floor and character sizes read clearly.
- Lead the eye with the architecture (a walkway, a table edge, a row of columns, the light pattern) to one focal point; the squint test must still show that focal point and the free space for the characters.
- Keep the backgrounds' values and patterns apart from where characters will stand: no busy pattern or high-contrast edge behind a head.
- Every receding edge goes to its vanishing point; furniture rotated to the room gets its own vanishing points on the same horizon.
- Parallax: draw the walls and floor complete behind the furniture (no holes when layers slide), run the far layer past the frame edges into the overscan, and keep the near layer to one or two framing objects.
- Cast shadows and contact shadows on everything that touches a surface; without them objects look pasted in.
Real-world sense (nothing absurd):
- The horizon is the one in the camera line; furniture sits ON the floor with contact shadows; nothing floats,
  intersects a wall or passes through another object.
- Sizes agree with the scale list: chairs fit under tables, doors are taller than people, screens and windows are
  the stated sizes, steps and sills are reachable.
- The set was drawn, not modelled: soft things have curved edges, chairs have shaped backs and seats, and no shape is
  an unexplained slab or patch.
- Every object reads at a glance and in silhouette as what it is (a chair as a chair, a plant as a real plant);
  every object listed in the scene is present, and nothing is there that would not be in this place.
- Light has one logic: every cast shadow falls away from the named source at a consistent angle; screens and lamps
  glow only if they are on in this version.
- No people, no letters, numbers or logos; slots are empty rects; the palette is exact.
Not in this style:
- clip-art furniture (generic shapes that could be any chair or any desk)
- every surface the same value, so nothing comes forward
- a centred, symmetrical, straight-on room with no depth
- rounded, inflated or pastel 'app onboarding' styling
- shadows that fall in different directions
- an empty, sterile room with no sign anyone works there
- objects with no cast shadow, which look copied and pasted in
Not in this world:
- a cartoon bank: no columns of gold bars, no money bags with dollar signs, no piles of coins, no round sci-fi vault doors
- exposed brick, small-paned steel factory windows, birch ply, brass desk lamps or deep green (they belong to another place)
- real brands, logos, signs with words, currency symbols, flags or anything that pins a country
- people in the sets (the cast is separate)
- words or numbers on screens, papers, leaflets or signs (empty slots only)
- screens facing a window or with a window directly behind them: screens sit at about 90 degrees to the windows
- sun patches (the street walls face north-west and the hour is late morning)
- a catalogue-clean bank: every scene shows that people work here
